{{convert|184.7|in|mm|0|abbr=on}} (MY1968){{cite web|url= http://www.gmheritagecenter.com/docs/gm-heritage-archive/vehicle-information-kits/Camaro/1968-Chevrolet-Camaro.pdf |work=GM Heritage Center |title=1968 Chevrolet Camaro - information kit |access-date=March 13, 2016}}
{{convert|186.0|in|mm|0|abbr=on}} (MY1969){{cite web|url= http://www.gmheritagecenter.com/docs/gm-heritage-archive/vehicle-information-kits/Camaro/1969-Chevrolet-Camaro.pdf |work=GM Heritage Center |title=1969 Chevrolet Camaro - information kit |date=September 1968 |access-date=March 13, 2016}} | width = {{unbulleted list|{{convert|72.5|in|mm|0|abbr=on}} (MY1967)|{{convert|72.5|in|mm|0|abbr=on}} (MY1968)|{{convert|74.0|in|mm|0|abbr=on}} (MY1969)}} | height = {{unbulleted list|{{convert|51.4|in|mm|0|abbr=on}} (MY1967)|{{convert|51.4|in|mm|0|abbr=on}} (MY1968)|{{convert|50.9|in|mm|0|abbr=on}} (MY1969 conv.)|{{convert|51.1|in|mm|0|abbr=on}} (MY1969)}} | designer = Henry Haga }} The '''first-generation [[Chevrolet Camaro]]''' is an American [[pony car]] introduced by [[Chevrolet]] in the fall of 1966 for the 1967 [[model year]]. It used a brand-new [[rear-wheel-drive]] [[GM F platform|GM F-body platform]] and was available as a 2-door, [[2+2 (car body style)|2+2]] seat, [[hardtop]], and [[convertible]]. The F-body was shared with the [[Pontiac Firebird]] for all generations. A 230 cu in [[Chevrolet Turbo-Thrift engine|Chevrolet straight-6]] was standard, with several Chevy [[V8]]s available as options.{{cite web|url= http://blog.hemmings.com/index.php/2011/07/06/down-the-throat-the-introduction-of-the-1967-camaro/ |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20111229025656/http://blog.hemmings.com/index.php/2011/07/06/down-the-throat-the-introduction-of-the-1967-camaro/ |url-status= usurped |archive-date= December 29, 2011 |title=Down the throat: the introduction of the 1967 Camaro|first=Daniel |last=Strohl |date=July 6, 2011 |work=Hemmings Daily |access-date=March 13, 2016}}{{cite magazine|last=Kilpatrick |first=Bill |title=The really new ones |magazine=Popular Mechanics |volume=126 |issue=4 |pages=105–108 |date=October 1966 |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=ydMDAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA105 |access-date=March 13, 2016}} The first-generation Camaro was built through the 1969 model year. Almost all of 1967–1969 Camaros were built in the two [[List of automotive assembly plants in the United States|U.S. assembly plants]]: [[Norwood Assembly|Norwood, Ohio]], and [[Van Nuys Assembly|Van Nuys, California]]. There were also five non-U.S. Camaro [[assembly plant]]s in countries that required local assembly and content. These plants were located in the Philippines, Belgium, Switzerland, Venezuela, and Peru.{{cite web|url= http://www.camaros.org/foreign.shtml |title=Camaro Foreign Assembly Plants |first=Kurt |last=Sonen |website=Camaros.org |date=November 26, 2013 |access-date=January 26, 2018}} ==Options== The debut Camaro's standard [[drivetrain]] was a Chevrolet Turbo-Thrift [[Chevrolet Turbo-Thrift engine#230|{{convert|230|cuin|L|1|abbr=on}} straight-6 engine]] rated at {{convert|140|hp|kW|0|abbr=on}} at 4400 rpm and {{convert|220|lbft|0|abbr=on}} of torque at 1600 rpm,{{cite web|url= http://www.automobile-catalog.com/car/1967/444380/chevrolet_camaro_sport_coupe_230_turbo-thrift_4-speed.html |website=Automobile-catalog.com |title=1967 Chevrolet Camaro Sport Coupe 230 Turbo-Thrift 4-speed |editor=Pawel Zal |access-date=2018-09-15}} coupled to a 3-speed manual transmission. To keep up with other manufacturers in the ever more crowded [[pony car]] niche, a selection of optional base-model and high-performance V8s was offered, as well as a variety of optional manual and automatic transmissions. Eight different engines were available in the 1967 Camaro, 10 in 1968, and 12 in 1969. Optional transmissions during the first-generation model run included the two-speed "[[Powerglide]]" [[automatic transmission]], and a four-speed manual, available with any engine.{{cite web |title=1967 Chevrolet Camaro brochure |website=oldcarbrochures.org |url= http://oldcarbrochures.org/United%20States/Chevrolet-Camaro/1967-Chevrolet-Camaro/1967_Chevrolet_Camaro_Brochure/slides/1967_Chevrolet_Camaro-14-15.html |page=15 |access-date=November 15, 2020}} A three-speed "[[Turbo-Hydramatic#THM350|Turbo Hydra-Matic 350]]" automatic became available on most V8s starting in 1968.{{cite web |title=1968 Chevrolet Camaro brochure |url= http://oldcarbrochures.org/United%20States/Chevrolet-Camaro/1968-Chevrolet-Camaro/1968-Chevrolet-Camaro-Brochure/slides/1968_Chevrolet_Camaro-15.html |website=oldcarbrochures.org |page=15 |access-date=November 15, 2020}} The optional automatic for SS 396 cars was the three-speed [[Turbo-Hydramatic#Super Turbine 400 / THM400 / THM375 / 3L80 / 3L80HD|Turbo 400]]. In 1969, a semi-automatic "Torque-Drive" two-speed transmission was available on six-cylinder models.{{cite web |title=1969 Chevrolet Camaro brochure (revised) |url= http://oldcarbrochures.org/United%20States/Chevrolet-Camaro/1969-Chevrolet-Camaro/1969-Chevrolet-Camaro-Brochure-Rev/slides/1969_Chevrolet_Camaro_Rev-15.html |website=oldcarbrochures.org |page=15 |access-date=November 15, 2020}} ===Packages=== The Camaro was offered in three main optional packages: * The '''RS''' appearance package. Available on any model, it included [[hidden headlights]] (with horizontally retractable doors that hid behind the grille when opened), revised [[taillight]]s with back-up lights under the rear [[Bumper (car)|bumper]], RS [[Badge|badging]], and bright exterior trim. * The '''SS''' performance package, consisting of a [[Chevrolet small-block engine (first- and second-generation)#350|{{convert|350|CID|L|1|abbr=on}}]] or [[Chevrolet small-block engine (first- and second-generation)#396|{{convert|396|cuin|L|1|abbr=on}}]] V8s and [[chassis]] upgrades to handle the additional power and deliver better [[Automobile handling|handling]]. The SS featured non-functional air inlets on the [[Hood (car)|hood]], special striping, and SS badging. * The '''Z/28''' performance package, designed to allow the Camaro to compete in the [[SCCA]] [[Trans-Am Series]]. It included a [[Hydraulic tappet|solid-lifter]] [[Chevrolet small-block engine (first- and second-generation)#302|{{convert|302|CID|L|1|abbr=on}} V8]], 4-speed transmission, power front [[disc brake]]s, 12-bolt rear axle, 15" wheels, heavy duty suspension and a pair of wide "skunk" [[Racing stripe|stripes]] down the hood and [[trunk lid]]. The Z/28 offered vibrant street-legal performance, but required numerous additional modifications to be raced competitively. == 1967 == [[File:1967 Chevrolet Camaro convertible, base six.jpg|thumb|left|1967 Camaro convertible, base six-cylinder model]] The 1967 styling was done by the same team that had designed the 1965 second-generation [[Chevrolet Corvair|Corvair]]. The Camaro shared the [[subframe]] / semi-[[unibody]] design with the 1968 [[Chevy II Nova]]. Almost 80 factory-and 40 [[Car dealership|dealer]]-installed options were offered, including the RS, SS, and Z/28 [[#Packages|main trim packages]]. ===SS=== The SS included a {{convert|350|cuin|L|1|abbr=on}} producing {{convert|295|bhp|PS kW|0|abbr=on}} at 4800 rpm and {{convert|380|lbft|Nm|0|abbr=on}} at 3200 rpm of [[Torque#Machine torque|torque]];{{cite web |url= https://www.carfolio.com/chevrolet-camaro-ss-277376?car=277376 |website=carfolio.com |title=1966 Chevrolet Camaro SS, 1967 MY |access-date=June 21, 2022}} and the ''L35'' and ''L78'' {{convert|396|cuin|L|1|abbr=on}} big-block [[V8 engine]]s producing {{convert|325|bhp|PS kW|0|abbr=on}} or {{convert|375|bhp|PS kW|0|abbr=on}} at 5600 rpm and {{convert|415|lbft|Nm|0|abbr=on}} at 3600 rpm of torque were available.{{cite web|url= https://www.carfolio.com/specifications/models/car/?car=277508 |website=carfolio.co |title=1966 Chevrolet Camaro SS, 1967 MY (396) |access-date=July 4, 2018}} The SS featured non-functional air inlets on the hood, special striping, and SS badging on the grille, front fenders, gas cap, and horn button. In 1967, a Camaro RS/SS convertible with a 396 engine [[Indianapolis 500 pace cars|paced the Indianapolis 500]]; 100 replicas were sold to the public.{{cite book|last=Flory |first=J. "Kelly" |title=American Cars, 1960-1972: Every Model, Year by Year |url= https://archive.org/details/americancarsever00flor_944 |url-access=limited |publisher=McFarland |year=2004 |isbn=9780786412730 |page=[https://archive.org/details/americancarsever00flor_944/page/n490 485]}} ===Z/28=== The Z/28 option code was introduced in December 1966 for the 1967 model year. It was the brainchild of Vince Piggins,{{who|date=February 2025}} who conceived offering "virtually race-ready" Camaros for sale from any Chevrolet dealer.''Rod Action'', 2/85, p.31. This option package was not mentioned in any sales literature, so it was unknown to most buyers.{{cite web|url= https://musclecars.howstuffworks.com/classic-muscle-cars/1967-chevrolet-camaro-z-28.htm |title=1967 Chevrolet Camaro Z28 |website=musclecars.howstuffworks.com |date=January 3, 2007 |access-date=June 21, 2022}} The Z/28 featured a high-output small-block [[Chevrolet small-block engine (first- and second-generation)#302|{{convert|302|cuin|L|1|abbr=on}} V8]] that had been designed for competing in the 5 litre (305 cu in) class of the then-popular [[Trans-Am Series|Trans-Am]] racing series. It had a strongly [[Stroke_ratio#Oversquare|over-square]], high-revving {{convert|4|in|1|abbr=on}} [[bore (engine)|bore]] and {{convert|3|in|1|abbr=on}} [[stroke (engine)|stroke]], with an aluminum [[intake manifold]], and a 4-barrel [[vacuum]] secondary high-volume 780 [[cubic feet per minute|cfm]] [[Holley Performance Products|Holley]] [[carburetor]]. It took Ford until 1969 to mount a head-to-head competitor: the [[Boss 302 Mustang]]. Advertised power of the 302 V8 was {{convert|290|hp|kW|0|abbr=on}} at 5300 rpm — intentionally under-rated (a common practice at the time) so Chevrolet could keep claimed [[horsepower]] under 1 per cubic inch for insurance premium calculations and racing classification. The Z/28 also came with upgraded suspension, [[power brakes|power]] front [[disc brakes]], a 4-speed [[List of GM transmissions#Manual transmissions|Muncie]] [[close-ratio transmission|close-ratio]] manual transmission and a 12-bolt rear axle. [[limited-slip differential|Positraction]] was optional. Wide racing stripes on the hood and trunk lid could be deleted at no charge, '302' front fender emblems came on the 1967 and early 1968 cars,{{cite web|url= http://www.camaros.org/geninfo.shtml#HowMany |title=Annual and Monthly Production Totals and VINs |website=camaros.org |access-date=June 21, 2022}} 'Z/28' emblems in the late 1968s and 1969s. The 1967 Z/28 received air from an open-element [[air cleaner]] or from an optional [[Air-mixing plenum|cowl plenum duct]] attached to the side of the air cleaner that ran to the firewall and got air from the cowl vents. An optional [[Hood scoop|cowl induction hood]] became available in 1969. 15-inch rally wheels were included with Z/28s, while all other 1967-9 Camaros had 14-inch wheels. [[File:Chevrolet Camaro (3) Travelarz.JPG|thumb|1968 Camaro interior]] The origin of the Z/28 nameplate came from the [[Regular Production Option|RPO codes]] – RPO Z28 was the code for the Special Performance Package. RPO Z27 was for the Super Sport package.{{citation needed|date=March 2024}} A total of 602 Z/28s equipped Camaros were sold in 1967. The Z/28 option would return in 1968, continue into the [[Chevrolet Camaro#Second generation (1970–1981)|second generation]] in 1970, drop the / from its name in 1972, and remain available as the Z28 through 1987. It would return for 1991 and continue to the end of the [[Chevrolet Camaro#Fourth generation|fourth generation]] in 2002. It would then reappear in 2014 in the [[Chevrolet Camaro#Fifth generation (2010–2015)|fifth generation]] rebadged back to the Z/28 (though 2015). There was no [[Chevrolet Camaro#Sixth generation (2016–2024)|sixth generation]] Z/28. === Swiss-assembled cars === Cars assembled in Switzerland, at GM's local facility in [[Biel/Bienne|Biel]], were all coupes with a Chevrolet [[Chevrolet small-block engine (first- and second-generation)#283|{{convert|283|cuin|L|1|abbr=on}} V8]] that produced {{convert|198|PS|kW hp|0|abbr=on}} at 4800 rpm and {{convert|285|lbft|0|abbr=on}} at 2400 rpm.{{cite web|title=1967 Chevrolet Camaro Sport Coupe V8 4-speed |url= https://www.automobile-catalog.com/car/1967/1823270/chevrolet_camaro_sport_coupe_v8_4-speed.html |website=automobile-catalog.com |access-date=June 21, 2022}} This engine was not available in contemporary Camaros built in the United States. The Swiss-built Camaros had a [[limited-slip differential]] and front disc brakes as standard. Some additional safety equipment was also standard. ===Production numbers=== {| |Base:||align="right"|121,051{{Citation needed|date=June 2025|reason=Reliable citation(s) needed for the model specific totals}} | |- |RS:||align="right" |64,842{{Citation needed|date=June 2025|reason=Reliable citation(s) needed for the model specific totals}} | |- |SS:||align="right"|34,411{{Citation needed|date=June 2025|reason=Reliable citation(s) needed for the model specific totals}} | |- |Z/28:||align="right"|602{{Citation needed|date=June 2025|reason=Reliable citation(s) needed for the model specific totals}} | |- |Total:||align="right"|220,906 | |} File:1967 Chevrolet Camaro Sport Coupe.JPG|1967 Chevrolet Camaro Sport Coupe File:1967 camaro ss 01.jpg|1967 Chevrolet Camaro SS convertible (with user-added Z/28 stripes, non-standard white-letter tires) File:1967 Chevrolet Camaro SS 396 coupe (19833939519).jpg|1967 Chevrolet Camaro RS/SS 396 coupé (with user-added Z/28 stripes, non-standard white-letter tires) {{clear}} == 1968 == [[File:1968 Camaro RS 327.jpg|thumb|1968 Camaro RS 327 (original optional stripe was black)]] [[File:1968CamaroSS.jpg|thumb|right|1968 Chevrolet Camaro SS convertible]] The styling of the 1968 Camaro was very similar to the 1967 design. With the introduction of Astro Ventilation, a fresh-air-inlet system, the side vent windows were deleted. Side marker lights were added on the front and rear fenders as part of safety requirements for all 1968 vehicles. Side mirrors changed from round to square. It also had a more pointed front grille and divided rear taillights. The front running lights (on non-RS models) were also changed from circular to oval. The SS models received chrome hood inserts that imitated [[velocity stack]]s and big block models had a low-gloss black rear tail light panel. The rear shock absorber mounting was staggered to resolve wheel hop issues, and higher-performance SS models received multi-leaf rear springs instead of single-leaf units. A {{convert|396|cuin|L|1|abbr=on}} producing {{convert|350|hp|kW|0|abbr=on}} at 5200 rpm and {{convert|415|lbft|0|abbr=on}} of torque at 3400 rpm big block engine was added as an option for the SS,{{cite web|url= http://www.automobile-catalog.com/car/1968/445775/chevrolet_camaro_ss-396_sport_coupe_350-hp_4-speed_close.html |title=1968 Chevrolet Camaro SS-396 Sport Coupe 350-HP 4-speed close |editor=Pawel Zal |access-date=2018-09-15}} and the Z/28 appeared in Camaro brochures, and nearly 7,200 were sold. The {{convert|427|cid|L|1|abbr=on}} was not available as a Regular Production Option (RPO). Chevrolet's Special Production Division had to convince Chevrolet's General Manager Pete Estes, but the General Manager only drove convertible vehicles, and the Z/28 was never produced as a convertible. A Central Office Production Order (COPO) was placed for the only Z/28 convertible Camaro built.{{cite web|url= https://www.wcshipping.com/blog/rarest-camaro-copo-1968-camaro-z28-convertible |title=Rarest Camaro: COPO 1968 Camaro Z/28 Convertible |first=Dmitriy |last=Shibarshin}} The car was parked in the executive garage which Pete Estes had access to. Upon driving the vehicle, he promptly approved promoting the Z/28. A 1968 Z/28 competed in the 1971 British Saloon Car Championship at Crystal Palace in a three-way battle for the lead, a race which was later featured in the "Sporting Moments" episode of BBC's ''[[100 Greatest (TV series)|100 Greatest]]'' series.{{cite web|url= https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cawBXWWgqCI |title=Film of Crystal Palace race in 1971 |date=25 February 2017 |via=YouTube}} === Production numbers === {| |Base: |159,087{{Citation needed|date=June 2025|reason=Reliable citation(s) needed for the model specific totals}} |- |RS:||align="right"|40,977{{Citation needed|date=June 2025|reason=Reliable citation(s) needed for the model specific totals}} |- |SS:||align="right"|27,884{{Citation needed|date=June 2025|reason=Reliable citation(s) needed for the model specific totals}} |- |Z/28:||align="right"|7,199{{Citation needed|date=June 2025|reason=Reliable citation(s) needed for the model specific totals}} |- |Total:||align="right"|235,147 |} {{clear}} == 1969 == [[File:1969 Chevrolet Camaro Pace Car.jpg|thumb|right|1969 Chevrolet Camaro Indianapolis 500 Pace Car Replica included the RS & SS options]] [[File:1969 red Chevrolet Camaro SS side.JPG|thumb|right|1969 Chevrolet Camaro SS]] The 1969 Camaro carried over the previous year's [[drivetrain]] and major mechanical components, but all-new [[sheet metal]], except the hood, trunk lid, and roof, gave the car a new look. The [[Grille (car)|grille]] was redesigned with sharper V and deeply inset headlights. New door skins, rear [[quarter panel]]s, and rear valance panel made the car look lower and wider. This styling would only serve for the 1969 [[model year]]. To increase competitiveness in the SCCA Trans-Am racing series, optional four-wheel disc brakes with four-piston calipers were made available during the year, under RPO JL8, for US$500.30.General Motors documentation This system used components from the Corvette and made for a significant improvement in the braking capability and was a key to winning the Trans-Am championship.{{citation needed|date=March 2024}} The option was expensive and only 206 units were produced. The Rally Sport (RS) option, RPO Z22, included a unique black-painted grille with concealed headlights and headlight washers, fender striping (except when sport striping or Z/28 Special Performance Package is specified), simulated rear fender [[louver]]s, front and rear wheel opening moldings, black body sill, RS emblems on grille, [[steering wheel]] and rear panel, Rally Sport front fender [[nameplate]]s, bright accented taillights, back-up lights below rear bumper; hardtops got bright roof drip moldings. The RS option cost $131.65, with 37,773 orders filled. Z/28 sales soared from 7,200 to over 20,000, available with the same {{convert|302|cuin|L|1|abbr=on}} small block producing {{convert|290|hp|PS kW|0|abbr=on}} at 5800 rpm and {{convert|290|lbft|0|abbr=on}} of torque at 4200 rpm.{{cite web|url= https://www.automobile-catalog.com/car/1969/446330/chevrolet_camaro_z28_sport_coupe.html |title=1969 Chevrolet Camaro Z28 Sport Coupe |website=automobile-catalog.com |editor=Pawel Zal |access-date=June 22, 2022}} It was backed by Muncie manual four-speed transmission with a new-for-69 standard [[Hurst Performance|Hurst]] [[Gear stick|shifter]] and connected to a 12-bolt [[rear axle]] with standard 3.73 gears. The 302 featured 11:1 compression, forged pistons, forged steel [[crankshaft]] and [[connecting rod]]s, [[valve lifter|solid lifters]], and Holley carburetor on a dual-plane intake manifold. A dual four-barrel crossram intake manifold was available as a dealer-installed option. [[File:Chevrolet Camaro Z28 1969 in Daytona Yellow.jpg|alt=1969 Chevrolet Camaro Z28 in Daytona Yellow|thumb|1969 Chevrolet Camaro Z28 in Daytona Yellow]] The 1969 model year was extended into November 1969, due to manufacturing problems that delayed the introduction of the [[Chevrolet Camaro#Second generation (1970–1981)|second generation]] model planned for 1970. === Production numbers === {| |Base:||align="right"|150,078{{Citation needed|date=June 2025|reason=Reliable citation(s) needed for the model specific totals}} |- |RS:||align="right"|37,773{{Citation needed|date=June 2025|reason=Reliable citation(s) needed for the model specific totals}} |- |SS:||align="right"|34,932{{Citation needed|date=June 2025|reason=Reliable citation(s) needed for the model specific totals}} |- |Z/28:||align="right"|20,302{{Citation needed|date=June 2025|reason=Reliable citation(s) needed for the model specific totals}} |- |Total:||align="right"|243,085 |} === COPO 427s === [[File:68 Yenko Camaro.jpg|thumb|1968 [[Yenko Camaro]]]] [[File:1969 Chevrolet Camaro COPO 9560 ZL1 (21363646465).jpg|thumb|1969 Camaro COPO 9560 ZL1]] A GM corporate edict forbade its Divisions from installing engines larger than {{convert|400|cid|L|1|abbr=on}} in mid-size and smaller models. Requests from dealers (notably [[Don Yenko]] in PA, Baldwin-Motion in NY, Nickey in IL and Dana in CA) who had been dealer-installing [[Chevrolet Big-Block engine#427|{{convert|427|cid|L|1|abbr=on}} engines]] in the Camaro prompted Chevrolet to use an ordering process usually used on fleet and special orders (taxis, trucks, etc.) to offer 427 engines in the Camaro. Two Central Office Production Orders (COPO), numbers 9560 and 9561, were offered in the 1969 model year.{{cite web|url= http://www.camaros.org/copo.shtml |title=COPO 427: The Relentless Pursuit of Acceleration |first=Bill |last=Glowacki |website=Camaros.org |date=June 5, 2014 |access-date=March 13, 2016}} The COPO 9561 used the cast iron block/cast iron heads, solid-lifter [[Chevrolet L72|L72]] big-block engine, rated at {{convert|425|hp|kW|0|abbr=on}} [[Horsepower#SAE gross power|SAE gross]] at 5600 rpm and {{convert|460|lbft|0|abbr=on}} of torque at 4000 rpm.{{cite web|url= https://www.ultimatecarpage.com/spec/4180/Chevrolet-Camaro-COPO-9561.html |website=Ultimatecarpage.com |title=Chevrolet Camaro COPO 9561 |editor-first=Wouter |editor-last = Melissen |date=December 2, 2009 |access-date=September 8, 2018}} Yenko ordered 201 of these cars to convert them into [[Yenko Camaro]]s.{{cite web|url= https://www.myclassicgarage.com/knowledge-base/1969-Chevrolet-Camaro |website=Myclassicgarage.com |title=1969 Chevrolet Camaro |access-date=September 8, 2018}} Other dealers also became aware of the L72 engine package. Around 1,000 Camaros were fitted with the L72 engine option.GM Tonawanda engine production data{{cite web |editor-last=Sonen |editor-first=Kurt |title=Camaro - 67-69 Camaro Model Information |url= http://www.camaros.org/model.shtml |website=camaros.org |access-date=November 15, 2020 |date=July 8, 2020}} The COPO 9560 used an all-aluminum [[Chevrolet big-block engine#ZL1|ZL1]] designed specifically for [[drag racing]], where weight savings were at an absolute premium. The package was conceived by drag racer Dick Harrell, and ordered through Fred Gibb Chevrolet in La Harpe, IL, to enter NHRA [[Super Stock (drag racing)|Super Stock racing]]. A total of 69 ZL1 Camaros were produced. The engine alone cost over US$4,000—or more than an entire base V8 Camaro. Rated at {{cvt|430|hp|kW|0}} [[Horsepower#SAE gross power|SAE gross]] at 5200rpm and {{cvt|450|lbft|0}} of torque at 4400rpm/{{cite web|url= http://www.superchevy.com/features/sucs-0707-1969-chevrolet-camaro-zl1/ |website=Superchevy.com |title=The 1969 ZL1 Camaro Legacy |editor-first=Paul | editor-last = Zazarine |date=July 26, 2007 |access-date=September 15, 2018}}{{cvt|376|hp|kW|0}} [[Horsepower#SAE net power|SAE net]] "as installed", it could produce over 500 gross with exhaust changes and [[Car tuning|tuning]]. The ZL1 engines were manufactured at the Tonawanda Assembly Plant before being installed in Corvettes and Camaros or sold over the counter to racers.''Auto Restorer'', December 2000, pp.14-15. Each took 16 hours to be hand-assembled in a room that Corvette Chief Engineer [[Zora Arkus-Duntov]] described as "surgically clean."{{cite book|title=Corvette: America's Star Spangled Sports Car |first=Karl E. |last=Ludvigsen |page=228 |year=1973 |publisher=Automobile Quarterly |isbn=9780525086451}} == First-generation engines == File:Chevrolet Camaro 1968 SS 396 Mouses LFront Engine TICO 13March2010 (14412845469).jpg|1968 SS 396 engine File:427 Aluminum in Camaro.jpg|427 aluminum engine File:69dz302.jpg|1969 Camaro Z28 only 302 Cubic inch, 290 Hp Engine. {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center;" !
